title: The Choice That Makes Code 1,000× Faster (or Slower)
subtitle: Same computer, same data, same task — but pick the wrong way to store your stuff and it grinds to a halt. Meet Big-O.
hook: Two programs do the exact same job on the exact same laptop. One finishes instantly; the other takes an hour. The difference isn't the CPU or the language — it's *how the data was organized* and *how the work scales as data grows*. This is the idea that makes senior engineers wince at junior code: **Big-O notation**, the language of 'how does this slow down as things get big?' Yesterday: where data lives. Today: how your choices scale.

builds_on.label: Why Your Computer Is Always Waiting

sections.heading: Big-O: how cost grows, not how long it takes
sections.body:
Big-O ignores the stopwatch and asks: **as the input gets N times bigger, how much more work?** A few flavors you'll meet everywhere:

- **O(1)** — constant. Same cost no matter how big N gets. (Grab item #5 from an array.)
- **O(log n)** — halve the problem each step. Blazing even for huge N. (Binary search.)
- **O(n)** — linear. Twice the data, twice the work. (Scan a list.)
- **O(n²)** — quadratic. 10× the data = **100×** the work. (Compare every pair — the junior-code trap.)

The magic isn't precision; it's seeing the *shape* of the growth before it bites you at scale.

sections.caption: As data grows, these curves diverge violently. O(n²) looks fine on 10 items and dies on 10,000.

sections.heading: This is why data structures exist
sections.body:
A **data structure** is just a way of organizing data so the operations you do most are cheap. Need instant lookup by key? A **hash table** gives ~O(1). Need to keep things sorted and searchable? A **tree** gives O(log n). Need order and fast ends? A **list** or **queue**. Choosing the right structure turns an O(n²) disaster into an O(n log n) breeze.

Hashing — turning a key into a location so you can jump straight to it — is so important it gets its own lesson later (and it's the seed of 'consistent hashing', which keeps giant systems from falling over). For now: **the structure you pick decides your Big-O.**

sections.caption: Big-O notation in about 6 minutes — the common curves, made intuitive.

takeaways: **Big-O** describes how work grows with input size N, not raw time.
Know the ladder: **O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n²)** — the last one explodes.
O(n²) hides on small inputs and detonates at scale — the classic trap.
A **data structure** organizes data so your common operations are cheap.
Pick the right structure (hash table, tree, list) and you pick your Big-O.

quiz.q: 10× more data makes an O(n²) algorithm roughly how much slower?
quiz.explain: Quadratic: (10)² = 100×. That's why O(n²) is fine on toy data and deadly at scale.

quiz.q: You need instant lookup of a value by its key. Best structure?
options: Scan a list every time — O(n)
quiz.explain: Hash tables jump straight to the key in ~constant time. The right structure sets your Big-O.

quiz.q: CALLBACK: Yesterday's lesson was about the memory hierarchy. How does it relate to Big-O?
options: Both are about speed: Big-O counts operations; the hierarchy sets how costly each memory touch is — real speed needs both
quiz.explain: Big-O counts steps; locality decides how slow each step's data access is. Fast code minimizes both.

tg_quiz.q: 10× the data into an O(n²) algorithm ≈ how much slower?
tg_quiz.correct: Yep — 100×. Quadratic bites hard at scale.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's 100× — (10)². That's why O(n²) is a trap.
tg_quiz.explain: Big-O is about how cost grows, not the raw clock.
